title: Fundamentals
note: The patterns behind most production data failures, as three chains: correctness, cost and operability, ending in a symptom-to-pattern diagnosis. Engine defaults are dated Nov 2026; refresh yearly.

concepts.s: Most production data failures trace to three chains: correctness (grain, keys, idempotent replay, time), cost (layout, then data movement) and operability (contracts, tests, freshness, ownership).

x.b:
• Correctness: what is one row? What identifies it? Can the job rerun safely? Which clock does it use?
  • Cost: how much is read (columnar layout, pruning, file sizes), then how much moves between machines (shuffle, skew, spill).
  • Operability: what was promised (contract), how it is checked (tests, freshness), who answers when it breaks (ownership, incidents).
Trap: Fixing the symptom layer. A wrong dashboard total is usually a grain or replay bug two layers down, not a BI bug.
"Revenue doubled overnight": correctness chain. Grain fan-out? Non-idempotent rerun? Duplicate delivery? Check in that order.

cards.q: A nightly job got 4x slower after volume doubled. Which chain do you inspect?
cards.a: Cost: layout and file sizes first, then shuffle, skew and spill.

cards.q: A metric is wrong only on days with a rerun. Which chain and link?
cards.a: Correctness: idempotent replay.

concepts.s: State in one sentence what one row represents, enforce it with a uniqueness test, and never join to a finer grain before aggregating.

x.b: The grain columns form the true key. Kimball's fact grains: transaction (one row per event), periodic snapshot (per entity per period), accumulating snapshot (per process instance, updated at milestones). Store the lowest atomic grain; you can roll up, never drill below it.
Trap: Join fan-out: one row per patient joined to one row per diagnosis, then summing visits, counts a three-diagnosis patient three times.

SELECT encounter_id, COUNT(*) FROM fct_encounters
GROUP BY encounter_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;  -- must return 0 rows

Compare row counts before and after every join.
What is one row, in one sentence, and which test enforces it?

cards.q: Totals are too high after adding a join to a diagnosis table. Most likely cause?
cards.a: Join fan-out: the diagnosis table has a finer grain, so rows multiply; aggregate it first.

cards.q: Why store facts at the lowest atomic grain?
cards.a: You can always aggregate up later but can never recover detail below the stored grain.

concepts.s: Facts hold measures at a declared grain, dimensions hold the context you filter by, and each measure's additivity decides how it may be aggregated.

x.b:
• Additive: sums across everything (minutes, revenue).
  • Semi-additive: not across time (balances, open caseload); use last value or average.
  • Non-additive: ratios; store numerator and denominator, divide at query time.

Conformed dimensions (one dim_date, one dim_provider) make cross-process reports agree. Star schemas suit semantic layers; Power BI's engine and DAX are designed around them.

Trap: Averaging stored percentages. The average of averages is wrong when group sizes differ.
Trap: Summing an end-of-month balance across months.
No-show rate by clinic: store no_shows and scheduled, then compute SUM(no_shows) / SUM(scheduled) at query time.

cards.q: Open caseload summed across 12 months gives a huge number. What went wrong?
cards.a: Caseload is semi-additive: it can't be summed over time; use the period-end value or an average.

cards.q: How should a rate be stored so any rollup is correct?
cards.a: As separate numerator and denominator columns, divided at query time.

concepts.s: Give dimension rows stable surrogate keys and version changing attributes as Type 2 rows, then join facts to the version valid at event time.

x.b:
• Type 1 overwrites (history lost); Type 2 closes the current row and inserts a new version with valid_from / valid_to and is_current.
  • Use half-open intervals [valid_from, valid_to) and a far-future end date for the open row.
  • Surrogate keys: a deterministic hash of source + natural key (+ valid_from) survives rebuilds; sequences get reassigned. Reserve -1 Unknown so facts never carry NULL keys.

Trap: Joining facts on natural key with is_current = true restates history to today's attributes.
Trap: Hashing churny columns (last_login) creates a new version every load.

ON f.provider_nk = d.provider_nk
 AND f.event_ts >= d.valid_from AND f.event_ts < d.valid_to

cards.q: Last year's report by clinic changed after providers moved clinics. What join mistake causes this?
cards.a: Joining on natural key with is_current = true instead of point in time against Type 2 validity ranges.

cards.q: Why prefer a deterministic hash surrogate key over a sequence?
cards.a: Rebuilds and backfills regenerate the same keys, so facts referencing them don't break.

concepts.s: Every job must leave the same final state no matter how many times it runs on the same inputs, because orchestrators retry and people rerun.

x.b:
• Patterns: overwrite the partitions you own, MERGE on key, delete-then-insert in one transaction, or stage and swap.
  • MERGE: deduplicate the source to one row per key, guard updates with a version check (s.seq > t.seq), skip no-op updates with a row hash.
  • Pass the run's logical date as a parameter; never use "today" in business logic.

Trap: Spark's default static partition overwrite with mode("overwrite") replaces the whole table. Use dynamic overwrite or replaceWhere.
Trap: Blind appends and non-deterministic row_number() tiebreaks.

(df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite")
   .option("replaceWhere", "event_date >= '2026-10-01' AND event_date < '2026-10-08'")
   .saveAsTable("silver.encounters"))
If this job runs twice, what changes? The answer must be nothing.

cards.q: MERGE fails with multiple source rows matching one target row. What is the fix?
cards.a: Deduplicate the source to one row per key, keeping the latest by a deterministic order.

cards.q: An older change overwrote a newer one during MERGE. What guard prevents it?
cards.a: A version check in the matched clause, e.g. WHEN MATCHED AND s.seq > t.seq.

concepts.s: Load only what changed since the last successful run, advancing the watermark after the write commits, with an overlap window because updated_at lies.

x.b:
1. Read the old watermark; capture the new upper bound first.
  2. Extract old < col <= new.
  3. Write idempotently.
  4. Advance the watermark only after commit.

updated_at misses rows: some writers skip it, timestamps are set before commit (long transactions land behind you), clocks skew, and deletes never appear. Mitigate with a lookback overlap plus idempotent MERGE, rowversion with MIN_ACTIVE_ROWVERSION() in SQL Server, periodic key reconciliation, or CDC.
Trap: Advancing the watermark before the write commits: a failed write skips that window forever.
Re-read the last hour on every run (col > wm - 1 hour); MERGE absorbs the repeats.

cards.q: Rows from a long-running transaction never reach the warehouse. Why?
cards.a: They committed with timestamps older than a watermark you had already passed; use an overlap window, or a rowversion watermark capped at MIN_ACTIVE_ROWVERSION().

cards.q: How does a timestamp watermark miss deletes, and what catches them?
cards.a: Deleted rows emit no change; periodic key reconciliation or CDC catches them.

concepts.s: Make every job a function of a date range so backfills and late-arriving data are just normal runs over older partitions.

x.b:
• Backfill: chunk by partition with bounded parallelism, write to a shadow table, reconcile, swap, rebuild dependents in order, warn consumers.
  • Late facts: reprocess a rolling lookback sized from measured lateness (p99 of ingest_ts - event_ts); deeper reconciliation for the rest.
  • Late dimensions: insert an inferred member flagged is_inferred, then update it in place when the real row arrives.

Trap: Backfilling with joins to current dimension state rewrites history.
Trap: Raw data retention shorter than your restatement window; keep bronze long enough to rebuild.
Publish a restatement policy: "the last 7 days may change; months close on the 5th business day", and show "data as of" on dashboards.

cards.q: Claims arrive up to 40 days late. How do you size the reprocessing window?
cards.a: From the measured lateness distribution (e.g. p99 of ingest minus event time), plus a deeper periodic reconciliation.

cards.q: A fact references a provider not yet in the dimension. What keeps the fact's key stable?
cards.a: An inferred member row, updated in place when the real provider row arrives.

concepts.n: Event time, processing time and streaming watermarks
concepts.s: Aggregate business questions by event time, keep ingest and processing timestamps beside it, and let a streaming watermark decide when a window is complete.

x.b:
• Keep event_ts, ingest_ts, processed_ts. Partition raw by ingest date; serve layers by event date.
  • Store UTC plus the source zone; convert to business days at the end (DST days have 23 or 25 hours).
  • A streaming watermark = max event time seen minus allowed lateness. Spark's append mode emits a window once the watermark passes its end and drops its state.

Trap: Grouping by processing time: an outage makes Tuesday empty and Wednesday huge.
Trap: Silent drops. Spark and Flink discard too-late events without error; reconcile against raw.

(events.withWatermark("event_ts", "15 minutes")
   .groupBy(window("event_ts", "5 minutes"), "clinic_id").count())

cards.q: One slow source stalls all output in a multi-stream Spark job. Why?
cards.a: Spark uses the minimum watermark across inputs by default, so the slowest stream holds everything back.

cards.q: What is the trade-off when raising allowed lateness?
cards.a: More complete results but higher latency and more state held in memory.

concepts.s: Exactly-once is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent or transactional sink, keyed by an ID created at the source.

x.b:
• At-most-once loses data; at-least-once duplicates; exactly-once means each effect lands once.
  • Delta's streaming sink skips replayed batches natively; in foreachBatch pass txnAppId and txnVersion, or MERGE on key.
  • Dedup key: a producer-assigned event ID; otherwise business key + version; content hash as a last resort.

Trap: IDs assigned at ingestion: each retry gets a new ID, so nothing deduplicates.
Trap: Hashing the whole row including ingest_ts or file name.
Trap: Side effects (emails, API calls) inside a batch are outside any engine guarantee.

QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id
  ORDER BY source_seq DESC, ingest_ts DESC) = 1

cards.q: Duplicates appear even though the pipeline claims exactly-once. Where do you look first?
cards.a: The sink: it must recognize replays (idempotent MERGE or transactional batch IDs), and the dedup key must come from the source.

cards.q: Exact replays vs updated versions: how does dedup differ?
cards.a: Replays keep the first copy; versions keep the latest by a deterministic ordering.

concepts.s: Read changes from the source's transaction log, apply them in log order with MERGE, and treat the snapshot-to-stream handoff as the riskiest moment.

x.b:
• Log-based CDC (Debezium, SQL Server CDC) captures deletes and every intermediate change with low source load; timestamp polling is not CDC.
  • SQL Server Change Tracking records only which keys changed; CDC keeps before and after values.
  • Per batch: collapse to the last change per key by log position (LSN), then MERGE. Tables need a primary key. Decide how deletes land.

Trap: Ordering by a timestamp column instead of log position (LSN, then sequence within a transaction).
Trap: Falling behind log retention: the only recovery is a full re-snapshot.
Initial load: take a consistent snapshot, record its LSN, stream from exactly that LSN. A gap or overlap here causes permanent drift.

cards.q: Within one CDC batch a row was updated three times. What do you apply?
cards.a: Only the last change per key by log position (LSN), via MERGE.

cards.q: Which source tables can't be applied reliably by CDC?
cards.a: Tables without a primary key.

concepts.s: Agree schema, meaning, quality and freshness with producers in code, be permissive at the raw edge and strict in the core, and quarantine bad records instead of failing or dropping them.

x.b:
• Safe: add a nullable column, widen a type. Breaking: rename, drop, narrow, change meaning (dollars to cents) with no schema change.
  • Avro/Protobuf registries check compatibility on publish; Iceberg tracks columns by ID so renames are metadata-only; Delta column mapping allows renames.
  • Bronze accepts new fields (Auto Loader's _rescued_data); silver and gold change only by review.
  • Dead-letter table: failing rows plus the reason, replayable after a fix.
Trap: Automatic schema evolution everywhere: a producer typo becomes a permanent gold column.
A contract test in the producer's CI fails their PR when a field the warehouse depends on is renamed, before it reaches you.

cards.q: amount switched from dollars to cents and nothing errored. What catches this?
cards.a: A data contract with semantic tests (range or distribution checks); schema checks alone can't.

cards.q: Bad rows arrive in a stream. Why route them to a dead-letter table rather than fail the job?
cards.a: Good data keeps flowing, and bad rows are kept with the reason for replay after a fix.

concepts.s: Most query cost is bytes read, so store columnar, filter on the columns the data is organized by, and let statistics skip files.

x.b:
• Columnar (Parquet): read only the columns you select; compression works per column.
  • Partition pruning: filters on partition columns skip whole folders. Partition only on low-cardinality columns queried constantly (usually date); Databricks advises not partitioning tables under about 1 TB and prefers liquid clustering.
  • Predicate pushdown and data skipping: min/max statistics let engines skip row groups and files; clustering (Z-order, liquid clustering) makes those ranges tight.

Trap: Wrapping the partition column in a function (WHERE year(event_date) = 2026) can defeat pruning.
Trap: Over-partitioning on high-cardinality keys creates millions of tiny files.
SELECT * on a 200-column table scans everything; selecting 6 columns with a date filter reads a fraction.

cards.q: A date-filtered query still scans the whole table. Two likely causes?
cards.a: The filter wraps the partition column in a function, or the table isn't partitioned or clustered on that column.

cards.q: When is a column a bad partition key?
cards.a: When it has high cardinality, which creates huge numbers of small files.

concepts.s: Keep files large and few with compaction, and use a table format (Delta, Iceberg) so every write is an atomic snapshot you can query back to.

x.b:
• Small files multiply metadata and task overhead; streaming and frequent appends create them.
  • Compaction (OPTIMIZE) rewrites them into large files; auto-compaction and optimized writes reduce the need.
  • Table formats add a transaction log: atomic commits, schema enforcement, time travel to a version, and concurrent writers.
  • VACUUM removes old files and with them the ability to time travel past retention.
Trap: Aggressive VACUUM retention breaks time travel and long-running readers.
A streaming table writes thousands of tiny files a day; schedule OPTIMIZE nightly and enable optimized writes.

cards.q: Queries on a streaming-fed table slow down week by week with the same data volume. Likely cause?
cards.a: Small-file accumulation; compact with OPTIMIZE or auto-compaction.

cards.q: What do you lose after VACUUM with a short retention?
cards.a: Time travel to versions older than the retention, and safety for long-running readers.

concepts.s: The most expensive thing a distributed engine does is move data between machines, so shrink, filter and broadcast before you join or group.

x.b:
• Joins, GROUP BY, DISTINCT and window functions trigger a shuffle across the network and disk.
  • Broadcast join: send a small table to every executor and skip shuffling the big one (Spark's automatic threshold, spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, defaults to 10 MB).
  • Adaptive Query Execution (on by default since Spark 3.2) can switch to broadcast and coalesce partitions at runtime.

Trap: Joining before filtering or aggregating, so the full volume crosses the network.
Trap: Broadcasting a table too large: out-of-memory on the driver or executors (Spark caps broadcasts at 8 GB).
Join 2 billion events to a 50k-row clinic table: broadcast the clinic table instead of shuffling the events.
Can this filter or aggregate run before the join?

cards.q: A join between a huge fact and a tiny lookup is slow. What do you check?
cards.a: Whether it broadcast the small side; if not, hint broadcast or raise the threshold.

cards.q: Which operations trigger a shuffle?
cards.a: Joins (non-broadcast), GROUP BY, DISTINCT, window functions and repartitioning.

concepts.s: When one task runs far longer than the rest, a few hot keys hold most of the data; when tasks write to disk mid-stage, partitions are too big for memory.

x.b:
• Skew: one key (an "unknown" provider, a giant customer) owns a huge share of rows. Fixes: AQE skew-join handling, filter or handle the hot key separately, salt the key.
  • Spill: partition data exceeds execution memory and is written to disk. Fixes: more or smaller partitions, filter earlier, larger memory per core.

Trap: Adding nodes to a skewed job. The one hot task still runs alone.
Trap: Default -1 Unknown keys collecting most rows and becoming the skewed key.
Spark UI: 199 tasks finish in 20 seconds, 1 takes 40 minutes. Check the key distribution: 30% of rows have provider_id = -1.

cards.q: One task takes 40 minutes while 199 take 20 seconds. Diagnosis and first fix?
cards.a: Skew on a hot key; enable AQE skew handling or handle or salt the hot key separately.

cards.q: The Spark UI shows heavy disk spill. Two fixes?
cards.a: Smaller or more partitions, and filtering or aggregating earlier (or more memory per core).

concepts.s: Attribute every dollar of compute to a pipeline and owner, then cut idle time, wasted reads and over-frequent schedules before buying anything.

x.b:
• Tag jobs and clusters by team and product; usage-billed platforms expose billing tables to query.
  • Biggest levers: auto-termination and serverless for spiky work, right-sized warehouses, incremental instead of full rebuilds, schedules matched to how fresh consumers need data.
  • Track cost per pipeline run and per consumer.

Trap: Hourly refreshes for a dashboard read once a day.
Trap: Full-history backfills on usage billing without an estimate.
A full nightly rebuild becomes an incremental MERGE of the last 3 days, cutting compute by an order of magnitude.

cards.q: A dashboard is read once each morning but its pipeline runs hourly. What's the fix?
cards.a: Match the schedule to consumer freshness needs: run it once before the morning read.

cards.q: What must exist before you can manage data platform cost?
cards.a: Attribution: tags or billing data that tie every job's cost to a pipeline and owner.

concepts.s: Test logic with fast unit tests, data with assertions at each layer, and the whole pipeline with a small end-to-end run, heaviest at the bottom.

x.b:
• Unit: transformation functions on tiny fixtures, in CI.
  • Data tests on every build: uniqueness on the grain, not-null keys, referential integrity, accepted values, row-count and volume bounds.
  • Integration: run the DAG on a sample in a non-production environment.
  • Reconciliation: totals against the source system.

Trap: Only end-to-end tests: slow, flaky, and they tell you something broke, not what.
Trap: Volume tests with fixed thresholds that alarm on every holiday.
dbt: unique and not_null on encounter_id, relationships to dim_patient, and a row-count check against yesterday within a seasonal band.

cards.q: Row counts dropped 40% overnight but every test passed. Which test layer was missing?
cards.a: Volume or anomaly checks (and reconciliation to source).

cards.q: Why keep most tests at the unit and data-test layers?
cards.a: They are fast and pinpoint what broke; end-to-end tests are slow and vague.

concepts.s: Promise freshness and correctness per dataset, watch them with lineage, give each dataset one owner, and run blameless postmortems when promises break.

x.b:
• Freshness SLA: data for day D is ready by time T. Alert on lag, not on job status.
  • Lineage: column-level lineage answers "what breaks if I change this?" and "where did this number come from?".
  • Ownership: one owning team per dataset, an on-call rotation for tier-1 data, runbooks.
  • Incidents: detect, communicate to consumers, mitigate, then a blameless postmortem with action items.
Trap: Green jobs, stale data. A job can succeed while reading an empty or unchanged source.
An alert fires when fct_encounters' latest event_date is older than 26 hours, routed to the owning team's on-call.

cards.q: Every job is green but the dashboard shows yesterday's data. What monitoring was missing?
cards.a: A freshness check on the data itself (latest event time), not just job status.

cards.q: What question does column-level lineage answer before a change?
cards.a: Which downstream tables, dashboards and metrics depend on this column.

concepts.s: Model pipelines as small, idempotent, parameterized tasks with explicit dependencies, and trigger on data availability rather than clock guesses.

x.b:
• One task, one output; pass the logical date as a parameter.
  • Dependencies on data (sensors, table-update triggers), not "run at 2am and hope".
  • Retries with backoff only for transient failures; fail fast on data errors.
  • Bounded concurrency so backfills don't starve production.

Trap: One giant task: a failure at step 9 reruns steps 1-8.
Trap: Retrying a non-idempotent task.
Gold builds when silver.encounters commits for date D, not at a fixed time that is sometimes too early.

cards.q: A gold job sometimes runs on incomplete data. What design change fixes it?
cards.a: Trigger on upstream data availability (sensor or table-update trigger) instead of a fixed clock.

cards.q: When should a task not be retried automatically?
cards.a: On data or logic errors, and whenever it isn't idempotent.

concepts.s: Ship pipeline code like application code: version it, test it in CI, and promote the same artifact through dev, test and prod with configuration, not edits.

x.b:
• Everything in Git: SQL, notebooks, job definitions, infrastructure.
  • CI runs unit and data tests on a pull request against sample data.
  • The same artifact is deployed to each environment; only parameters (connections, schemas, sizes) change.
  • Production writes only through the deployment pipeline's identity.

Trap: Hand-editing jobs in production: the next deploy silently reverts the fix.
Trap: Dev reading production PHI.
A pull request builds a bundle, runs tests on a dev schema, and after merge the same bundle deploys to prod with the prod parameter file.

cards.q: A hotfix made in the production UI disappeared after the next release. Why?
cards.a: Production wasn't deployed only from Git; the release overwrote the hand edit.

cards.q: What may differ between environments in a sound promotion?
cards.a: Only configuration: connections, schema names, sizes, secrets.

concepts.s: Separate raw (bronze), cleaned and conformed (silver) and consumption-ready (gold) layers so you can always replay from raw and change one stage at a time.

x.b:
• Bronze: append-only copy of the source, by ingest date, kept long enough to rebuild.
  • Silver: typed, deduplicated, conformed entities at their natural grain.
  • Gold: facts, dimensions and aggregates shaped for consumers and the semantic layer.

Trap: Business logic in bronze, or consumers reading silver directly: both freeze internals into contracts.
Trap: Layers as ritual: three copies of the same table with no change between them.
A bug in deduplication is fixed in silver and replayed from bronze; gold rebuilds downstream with no source re-extract.

cards.q: A transform bug corrupted silver for a month. What lets you recover without the source?
cards.a: An immutable bronze layer kept long enough to replay.

cards.q: Who should read silver tables directly?
cards.a: Mostly engineers; consumers read gold so silver internals can change.

concepts.s: Define each business metric once, with owner, grain and filters, in a governed semantic layer so every tool reports the same number.

x.b:
• A metric definition: name, formula, grain, filters, time logic, owner.
  • Live in one place (Power BI semantic models, the dbt Semantic Layer, Databricks metric views) and expose it to every tool.
  • Certify a small set of tier-1 metrics; everything else is exploratory.
Trap: The same metric defined in five dashboards with five filters, then a meeting about whose number is right.
"Active patient": at least one completed visit in the trailing 12 months, by visit date, excluding test accounts; owned by clinical ops.

cards.q: Two executives bring different active-patient counts. What is the structural fix?
cards.a: One governed metric definition in a semantic layer with an owner, used by every tool.

cards.q: What must a metric definition specify beyond its formula?
cards.a: Grain, filters, time logic and an owner.

concepts.s: Treat protected health information with least privilege by default: classify it, mask or tokenize it outside its purpose, audit access, and keep it out of lower environments.

x.b:
• Classify columns (tags) at ingestion; drive masking and row filters from the tags.
  • Minimum necessary: analysts get de-identified or masked data unless their role needs identifiers.
  • Audit logs on who read what; retention and deletion rules per dataset.
  • Vendors handling PHI sign a BAA.

Trap: Copying production to dev for testing. Use synthetic or de-identified data.
Trap: PHI in logs, error messages and dead-letter tables.
A column tagged phi.mrn is masked for every group except care operations, and each query against it lands in the audit log.

cards.q: A dead-letter table stores full failing records from a patient feed. What is the risk?
cards.a: PHI leaks outside its governed tables; mask or restrict the dead-letter store too.

cards.q: What principle sets who sees identifiers?
cards.a: Minimum necessary: only roles that need identifiers get them; others see masked or de-identified data.

concepts.s: Diagnose by mapping the symptom to the chain it belongs to, then test the most common cause in that chain first.

x.b:
• Total too high: join fan-out, duplicate delivery, non-idempotent rerun.
  • Total too low: inner join to a dimension missing members, watermark skip, late data outside the window, silent streaming drops.
  • History changed: is_current join, Type 1 overwrite, backfill with current dimensions.
  • Slow: no pruning, small files, shuffle of the big side, skew, spill.
  • Stale but green: missing freshness check, upstream empty.
Trap: Patching the dashboard. Fix the layer that produced the error and add a test there.
Counts low only for new clinics: the inner join to dim_clinic drops rows whose clinic isn't loaded yet. Use -1 Unknown or inferred members.

cards.q: Counts are low only for newly onboarded clinics. Most likely cause?
cards.a: An inner join to a dimension that lacks the new members; use Unknown keys or inferred members.

cards.q: Last quarter's numbers changed after a dimension update. Most likely cause?
cards.a: Facts joined on is_current or a Type 1 overwrite instead of point-in-time Type 2.
